title: ACCA BT - Business and Technology
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the ACCA BT syllabus study guide. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: A physiotherapist runs her own practice, keeps all the profits, and is personally liable for all debts of the business. Which type of business organisation is she operating?
items.explanation: A sole trader is an individual who runs a business alone, keeps the profits, and has unlimited liability. A company would give limited liability but involves incorporation and shareholders.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: A company's shareholders lose only the amount they invested even if the business cannot pay its debts. Which characteristic of a limited company explains this protection?
options: Separate legal personality and limited liability
items.explanation: A company is a separate legal person from its owners, so shareholders' liability is limited to the amount unpaid on their shares. This is the defining advantage of incorporation.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: A charity considers not only its beneficiaries and donors but also its volunteers, employees, and the local community when making decisions. Which concept does this broad consideration describe?
items.explanation: Stakeholder theory holds that a business should consider all groups affected by its activities, not only shareholders. Agency theory instead describes the relationship between owners and managers.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: A hospital uses a grid that plots stakeholders by their power to influence and their interest in the organisation, then picks a communication strategy for each. Which model is being applied?
items.explanation: Mendelow's matrix classifies stakeholders by power and interest to guide engagement, such as keeping some satisfied and others closely managed. Porter's five forces and the BCG matrix address strategy instead.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: A small firm has very few layers of management and each manager supervises many employees directly, which speeds up decisions and communication. Which feature describes this structure?
items.explanation: A flat structure with few layers gives managers a wide span of control over many subordinates. Tall structures have narrow spans and more layers of authority.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: An engineering consultancy assigns each engineer to both a functional department and a project team, so engineers report to two managers at once. Which organisational structure does this create?
items.explanation: A matrix structure combines functional and project-based reporting so employees have two bosses. This improves flexibility but can create conflicting instructions and complex accountability.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: A retail chain gives store managers authority to choose product ranges, set local prices, and hire staff without asking head office. Which approach is the chain using?
items.explanation: Decentralisation pushes decision-making authority down to local managers who are closer to customers. Centralisation would keep those decisions at head office instead.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: A marketing team rewrites its target so that it can be measured and delivered within a specific timeframe, rather than remaining vague. Which characteristic of a good objective is being applied?
items.explanation: SMART objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. Making a target measurable and time-bound directly applies the SMART test.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: A company publishes a short statement describing its purpose, what it aims to achieve, and the values that guide its decisions. Which document is this?
items.explanation: A mission statement sets out an organisation's purpose, values, and long-term aims. Cash budgets, audit reports, and balance sheets are financial documents, not statements of purpose.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: A board of directors allocates responsibility for overseeing the external audit and the integrity of financial reporting to a specialist committee. Which committee is this?
items.explanation: An audit committee oversees financial reporting, internal controls, and the external auditor. Remuneration and nomination committees address executive pay and board appointments respectively.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: Shareholders appoint directors to run the company, but shareholders cannot observe every decision the directors make. Which governance issue arises from this separation of ownership and control?
items.explanation: The agency problem arises because managers as agents may act in their own interests rather than the shareholders' interests under imperfect information. Governance mechanisms aim to align these interests.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.stem: A finance manager needs a single definition of corporate governance for a training slide. Which definition is most widely accepted in governance codes?
options: The process of preparing annual financial statements
The marketing of shares to new investors
The day-to-day management of production schedules
The system by which organisations are directed and controlled
items.explanation: Corporate governance is commonly defined as the system by which companies are directed and controlled, covering board structures, accountability, and shareholder relations. The other options describe operations.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Organisation Structure and Governance

items.domain: Business Functions and the Wider Environment
items.stem: A manufacturer reviews the effect of a new minimum wage law, import tariffs, and a consumer trend toward organic products on its plans. Which analysis framework covers these external influences?
items.explanation: PESTEL analyses Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, and Legal forces in the wider environment. Minimum wage law and tariffs are political and legal, while the organic trend is social.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Functions and the Wider Environment

items.domain: Business Functions and the Wider Environment
items.stem: A component supplier is squeezed because a handful of large customers place very few, very large orders and can demand constant price cuts. Which of Porter's five forces is strongest here?
items.explanation: Large customers buying in high volume hold strong bargaining power over suppliers, enabling them to force prices down. The description points to buyer power rather than substitutes or entrants.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Functions and the Wider Environment

items.domain: Business Functions and the Wider Environment
items.stem: An HR manager establishes a pool of qualified applicants for a vacant role and then uses interviews to choose the best candidate from that pool. Which two HR activities are being performed in sequence?
items.explanation: Recruitment attracts and builds a pool of candidates, while selection chooses the best person from that pool. Training and appraisal come after the appointment is made.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Functions and the Wider Environment

items.domain: Business Functions and the Wider Environment
items.stem: A cosmetics brand finalises its product range, sets retail prices, chooses distribution channels, and plans promotion campaigns for the launch. Which marketing concept combines these four decision areas?
items.explanation: The marketing mix or four Ps are product, price, place, and promotion. The scenario describes all four decision areas, so the marketing mix is the correct concept.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Functions and the Wider Environment

items.domain: Business Functions and the Wider Environment
items.stem: An insurer divides the population into student, young professional, family, and retiree groups and designs a different policy for each group. Which marketing strategy is the insurer using?
items.explanation: Market segmentation splits a market into groups with distinct needs and tailors an offer to each. Mass marketing would offer one identical product to the entire market.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Functions and the Wider Environment

items.domain: Business Functions and the Wider Environment
items.stem: A car manufacturer schedules components to be delivered by suppliers only when they are needed on the production line, reducing inventory holding. Which operations technique does this describe?
items.explanation: Just-in-time eliminates waste by receiving materials only when required for production, cutting inventory and storage costs. TQM focuses on quality and kaizen on continuous improvement.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Functions and the Wider Environment

items.domain: Business Functions and the Wider Environment
items.stem: A food processor believes that quality should be built into every process and that defects should be prevented rather than checked and reworked at the end. Which operations philosophy is this?
items.explanation: Total quality management makes everyone responsible for quality and emphasises prevention by doing it right first time. Piecework, division of labour, and batch production do not address quality ownership.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Functions and the Wider Environment

items.domain: Business Functions and the Wider Environment
items.stem: A factory improves pay and working conditions, and workers stop complaining, but motivation does not increase. According to Herzberg, how should management view these improved factors?
options: Hygiene factors that remove dissatisfaction but do not motivate
items.explanation: Herzberg's hygiene factors such as pay and conditions prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate. Motivation requires satisfying factors like achievement, recognition, and responsibility.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Functions and the Wider Environment

items.domain: Business Functions and the Wider Environment
items.stem: A new employee demands safe working conditions and job security before he is willing to worry about being promoted. Which need level in Maslow's hierarchy must be satisfied first?
items.explanation: Maslow places safety needs immediately above physiological needs; job security and safe conditions belong to this level. Esteem and self-actualisation are pursued only after lower needs are met.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Functions and the Wider Environment

items.domain: Business Functions and the Wider Environment
items.stem: A quality manager distinguishes between inspecting finished goods to find faults and designing systems so that faults do not happen in the first place. Which pair of terms matches this distinction?
items.explanation: Quality control uses inspection and testing to detect defects, while quality assurance focuses on prevention through robust systems and processes. The sequence matches control followed by assurance.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Business Functions and the Wider Environment

items.stem: A sales manager transforms thousands of raw order records into a monthly summary that helps decide which products to discontinue. How is the monthly summary best described?
options: A transaction, because it records a sale
Information, because it is meaningful and useful for decisions
items.explanation: Information is data that has been processed and given meaning so it supports decision making. Raw order records are data, while the summarised monthly report is information.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: A bank's computer system records every customer deposit and withdrawal as it happens, updating account balances instantly. Which information system is performing this role?
items.explanation: A transaction processing system records routine, high-volume day-to-day transactions such as deposits and withdrawals. Decision support and executive systems serve analysis and planning instead.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: A production manager receives weekly reports on output, scrap, and machine utilisation that let her monitor performance against targets. Which system typically produces these routine reports?
items.explanation: A management information system turns transaction data into regular summary reports for monitoring and control. Transaction systems record activity, while expert systems offer specialist advice.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: A finance analyst uses software to run what-if models comparing the profit effect of different price and cost scenarios. Which system supports this semi-structured decision making?
items.explanation: A decision support system helps managers model alternatives and analyse semi-structured problems such as pricing scenarios. Payroll and point-of-sale systems are routine transaction systems.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: The CEO of a conglomerate wants a dashboard that summarises the group's performance and highlights exceptions for the most senior leaders. Which system is most appropriate?
items.explanation: An executive information system gives senior managers concise, exception-based summaries of organisation-wide performance. Routine transaction systems are designed for operational staff.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: A retailer collects massive amounts of data generated at high speed in many formats, including social media posts, till scans, and video. Which term describes the sheer scale, speed, and variety of these datasets?
items.explanation: Big data is characterised by its high volume, high velocity, and high variety. Data mining is the analytical technique applied to such datasets rather than the datasets themselves.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: A small business uses an accounting program that runs in the supplier's data centre and is accessed over the internet, so the firm installs nothing on its own computers. Which deployment model is this?
items.explanation: Software as a service delivers applications over the internet, hosted in the supplier's infrastructure and usually on subscription. On-premise software would be installed and run locally.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: A company collects customers' email addresses for order confirmation and promises not to use them for any other purpose without consent. Which data protection principle is the company following?
items.explanation: Purpose limitation requires personal data to be collected for specified, legitimate purposes and not used for incompatible ones. This mirrors the obligation to use data only for the purpose it was collected.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: An employee receives an email that appears to come from the bank and asks her to click a link and enter her password. Which security threat is she facing?
items.explanation: Phishing uses deceptive emails or links to trick people into revealing login credentials or personal data. DDoS, SQL injection, and man-in-the-middle attacks are technical rather than social engineering.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: A hospital's file server is encrypted by a program that demands a payment before the files can be unlocked. Which type of malicious software has attacked the server?
items.explanation: Ransomware encrypts a victim's data and demands payment for the decryption key. Spyware and keyloggers are designed to observe, and adware to display advertising, not to lock data.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: A bank requires the employee who issues payment orders to be different from the employee who records them in the ledger, so no single person controls a transaction from start to finish. Which internal control is this?
items.explanation: Segregation of duties splits incompatible tasks among different people to reduce the risk of error or fraud. Physical security and budgetary control address different control needs.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: An IT administrator gives each employee access only to the files and functions needed for their own job, rather than all company data. Which access control principle is being applied?
items.explanation: Least privilege grants users only the access necessary to perform their roles, limiting the damage of misuse or account compromise. The alternative would be broad or unrestricted access.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: A purchasing manager must approve every order above a fixed amount before it can be placed with a supplier. Which internal control activity does this approval represent?
items.explanation: Authorisation is a preventive control requiring managerial approval before transactions proceed. Reconciliation checks records against external evidence, and segregation splits duties among people.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.stem: A firm stores nightly copies of its data at an off-site location so that operations can be restored if its main server room is destroyed. Which plan does this support?
items.explanation: A disaster recovery plan sets out how systems and data will be restored after a disruptive event such as fire, flood, or cyberattack. Off-site backups are a key element of such a plan.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - Technology and Data in Business

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: An accountant reports monthly cost variances to production managers to help them control spending, while another prepares the annual statutory accounts. Which two branches of accounting are being described?
items.explanation: Management accounting provides internal information for planning and control, while financial accounting reports to external stakeholders in statutory accounts. The order matches management then financial.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: A finance director explains that one part of the function prepares reports primarily for internal managers, while another directs its reports at shareholders and regulators. Which statement best summarises the difference?
options: Management accounting serves internal decision makers; financial accounting reports to external parties
Financial accounting serves internal managers; management accounting reports to shareholders
Both branches serve only the tax authority
items.explanation: Management accounting is forward-looking and tailored for internal managers, while financial accounting is historic, regulated, and aimed at external users such as shareholders and regulators.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: A company records revenue when goods are delivered to customers even though cash will arrive later, and records expenses in the period they are incurred. Which accounting concept governs this treatment?
items.explanation: The accruals and matching concept recognises income and expenses when they occur rather than when cash changes hands, so they are matched to the period they relate to. The other concepts address different assumptions.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: An accountant values inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value so that profits and assets are not overstated. Which accounting concept supports this cautious treatment?
items.explanation: Prudence requires caution in estimates so that assets and income are not overstated and liabilities are not understated. Lower-of-cost-and-net-realisable-value is the classic application of prudence.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: A trainee accountant refuses to sign a report she knows contains false claims about a client's financial position. Which fundamental ethical principle is she upholding?
items.explanation: Integrity requires accountants to be straightforward and honest and to avoid being associated with misleading information. Refusing to sign a false report directly upholds integrity.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: An auditor receives an expensive gift from the client's finance director shortly before the annual audit opinion is signed. Which fundamental principle is most at risk from accepting the gift?
items.explanation: Objectivity requires judgement to be free from bias or conflict of interest. A significant gift or hospitality from a client could compromise the auditor's impartiality and independence.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: While working for a client, an accountant learns of a planned takeover and tells a family member, who then buys shares. Which fundamental ethical principle has been breached?
items.explanation: Confidentiality forbids disclosing information acquired through professional work without proper authority, especially for personal use. Passing the takeover information to a family member breached that duty.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: A newly qualified accountant takes on an audit of a complex pension scheme having no training or experience in that area, hoping to learn while working. Which principle has the accountant failed to apply?
items.explanation: Professional competence and due care requires accountants to act diligently and to accept only work they are competent to perform. Taking on unfamiliar specialist work without preparation breaches it.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: An accountant preparing a purchase decision is paid a bonus only if the company buys equipment from a particular supplier. Which category of ethical threat does this financial incentive create?
items.explanation: A self-interest threat arises when a financial or other personal interest could bias professional judgement. The bonus creates a direct interest in the outcome of the purchase decision.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: A firm is asked to audit systems that the same firm's consulting team designed and implemented for the client the previous year. Which ethical threat is most likely?
items.explanation: A self-review threat arises when an accountant evaluates their own previous work, which can compromise objectivity. Safeguards may include using different teams or an independent second-partner review.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: An accounting firm requires client acceptance files to be reviewed by the audit partner and prohibits gifts above a trivial value to reduce the chance of bias. Which term describes these measures?
items.explanation: Safeguards are actions taken to eliminate or reduce ethical threats to an acceptable level, such as approvals, prohibitions on gifts, and independence reviews. The other options are not protective measures.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: An accounts clerk suspects her employer is misstating its accounts and reports it to the external auditor and the relevant regulator. Which course of action has the clerk taken?
items.explanation: Whistleblowing is reporting suspected wrongdoing to proper authorities in the public interest. It is permitted and may even be required, and is distinct from unauthorised disclosure for personal advantage.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: A bank's compliance officer checks customer identities and reports suspicious cash deposits to the financial intelligence unit. Which legal responsibility is the officer fulfilling?
items.explanation: Anti-money laundering duties include customer due diligence on identity and reporting suspicious transactions. Detecting and reporting money laundering is a key compliance duty of financial institutions.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics

items.domain: The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
items.stem: A corporate governance code recommends that one individual should not combine the roles of chair and chief executive in a listed company. Which governance concern does this separation address?
options: Preventing a concentration of unchecked power
items.explanation: Combining the chair and chief executive roles concentrates power in one person and weakens board scrutiny. Separating the roles improves checks and balances and accountability to shareholders.
items.reference: ACCA BT Syllabus Study Guide - The Accountant in Business and Professional Ethics
